passage:
Monday. Vaibhav clapped just as Indu, his mother, switched on the ceiling fan. He stared up, then clapped again, harder.
Wednesday. He waved at his toy car the moment his cousin pressed the remote. Vrrm! Vaibhav squealed and waved at everything: the car, the door, a spoon.
Friday. At the lift, Vaibhav held up both hands and wiggled his fingers. The doors slid open. He turned to Indu, beaming. "Me!"

qa.q: What did Indu switch on as Vaibhav clapped?
qa.a: The ceiling fan.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav seem to believe when the lift doors opened?
qa.a: Vaibhav seemed proud and delighted, believing his wiggling fingers opened the doors, since he turned to Indu beaming and said 'Me!'

qa.q: How could Indu respond to 'Me!' in a way that fits his age?
qa.a: Share his joy, then show him simply, like pressing the lift button together, so he slowly learns what really makes things move.

qa.q: How might the cousin see Vaibhav waving at everything?
qa.a: The cousin might find it funny and even press the remote on purpose to hear him squeal. 🙂

grounding: Across a week, a toddler boy acts as if his claps and waves make the fan, a toy car and lift doors move.

passage:
On the balcony of their Hyderabad flat, two-year-old Reyansh pointed at the dark street and shouted, "Light!" At that exact moment, the streetlamps flickered on.
He gasped and grabbed Aditi's dupatta. "Light!" he shouted at the sky, then at the moon, then at the neighbour's window.
His big sister Ishita giggled. "He thinks he's switching them on, Mumma."
The next evening Reyansh was at the balcony early, finger ready, waiting.

qa.q: What happened the moment Reyansh shouted 'Light!'?
qa.a: The streetlamps flickered on.

qa.q: Why was Reyansh at the balcony early the next evening?
qa.a: Reyansh seemed excited and eager, believing his shout had turned the lamps on, and he wanted to do it again.

qa.q: What could Aditi do the next evening?
qa.a: Enjoy the moment with him, say simply that the lamps come on by themselves when it gets dark, and let him press a light switch indoors that he really can control.

qa.q: How does Ishita see her brother's shouting?
qa.a: She finds it sweet and funny, and understands he thinks he's switching the lamps on.

grounding: A two-year-old boy shouts at the moment streetlamps come on and acts as if his word made it happen.

passage:
"Lalit, why are you blowing at the TV?"
"Go off!"
"You wanted it off?" asked Chaitanya, kneeling beside him.
"Me blow. It go off."
"Beta, Dadi switched it off with the remote. Look, here's the remote."
"No! Me blow!"
"Okay. Blow again."
Lalit puffed out his cheeks. Pff! The screen stayed dark.
"Hmm. Blowing didn't work this time. Want to press the red button?"
Click. The screen lit up. Lalit's eyes went wide. "Again!"

qa.q: Who switched off the TV with the remote?
qa.a: Dadi.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the TV going off?
qa.a: Lalit felt proud, sure his own blowing had switched it off; he insisted 'Me blow!' even after hearing about the remote.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that suits a toddler?
qa.a: He didn't argue; he let Lalit test the blowing, then offered the real red button, so Lalit could see the cause for himself.

qa.q: What might Dadi think if she heard Lalit's claim?
qa.a: She would probably smile, knowing she pressed the remote while he was blowing.

grounding: A toddler boy believes his blowing switched off the TV, and a family member lets him test it and then shows the real button.

passage: Daycare note, Wednesday. Kiran (2) sat by the toy train while it ran on its track. When it stopped, he waved both hands hard and shouted, "Go!" Aunty Baljeet had just switched it back on, so it moved. He beamed and waved again at the next stop. Later he waved at the window when the rain stopped too. We smiled and played along, and I showed him the switch. He waved anyway. — Baljeet

qa.q: What did Kiran shout when the toy train stopped?
qa.a: "Go!"

qa.q: Why did Kiran beam when the train moved again?
qa.a: He believed his waving had made the train go, because it moved right after he waved.

qa.q: What gentle step did the caregiver take to help Kiran?
qa.a: The caregiver played along and also showed him the switch, giving a simple true reason without spoiling his fun.

qa.q: How might the caregivers feel watching Kiran wave at the rain?
qa.a: They probably find it sweet and amusing, knowing that at two he can't yet tell his wishes from what makes things happen.

grounding: A caregiver notes a toddler who believes his wave makes a toy train move and the rain stop.

passage: At dusk in their village near Nashik, Kamal, two, stood at the gate with his sister Arohi. The cows were far off in the field. "Come!" Kamal shouted, waving his arms. Slowly, the cows turned and walked home, as they did every evening. Kamal squealed and clapped. "I called!" Then the bus horn sounded down the road. Kamal clapped again, and the bus came around the corner. He looked up at Arohi, eyes huge. Arohi laughed and picked him up.

qa.q: What did Kamal shout at the cows?
qa.a: "Come!"

qa.q: Why did Kamal think he had called the cows home?
qa.a: He waved and shouted just before they walked back, so to him it looked like his call made them come.

qa.q: How could Arohi gently show Kamal what really brings the cows home?
qa.a: She could walk with him tomorrow at the same time and point out that the cows come every evening, even before he calls.

qa.q: What might Arohi be thinking when Kamal looks up at her with huge eyes?
qa.a: She probably finds his belief funny and sweet, knowing the cows and bus come every evening anyway.

grounding: A toddler in a village believes his call and clap bring the cows and bus, unable to separate his wish from what happens.

passage:
"Fan go!" Jomon waved both hands at the ceiling.
In the kitchen doorway, Dilnaz aunty flicked the switch. The fan began to turn.
Jomon's mouth fell open. "Jomon did it!"
"You did?" said Dilnaz aunty, smiling.
He waved again. "Fan stop!"
She switched it off. The blades slowed.
Jomon squealed and flapped his arms. "Fan go! Fan go!"
Dilnaz aunty laughed and switched it on once more. "Clever boy. Now, shall we find your ball?"

qa.q: What did Jomon wave at?
qa.a: He waved both hands at the ceiling fan.

qa.q: Why did Jomon squeal and flap his arms?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and proud because he believed his waving made the fan start and stop.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz aunty do next time to gently show how the fan works?
qa.a: She could let Jomon watch her press the switch, or help him press it himself, so he sees what makes it go.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz aunty feel playing the game with Jomon?
qa.a: She seems amused and fond, enjoying his delight while she works the switch.

grounding: Shows a toddler believing his wave makes the ceiling fan move, unable to separate his gesture from what really happens.

passage:
Daycare note, Holi week.
At five the courtyard lights came on by timer, just as Raghav clapped. He stared at his hands and clapped again. All evening he clapped at every lamp and the fan. When nothing happened, he clapped harder, with Chetan giggling beside him in colour-stained kurtas. Tomorrow I will let Raghav press the switch with me, so he can feel what really turns the lights on. 🙂

qa.q: At what time did the courtyard lights come on?
qa.a: At five, on their usual timer.

qa.q: Why did Raghav clap harder when nothing happened?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and determined, because he believed his clap had caused the lights and expected it to work again.

qa.q: Why is letting Raghav press the switch a good next step?
qa.a: It lets him feel the real cause with his own hands, gently showing that the button, not his clap, lights the lamps.

qa.q: What might the clapping game be like for Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan seems to be enjoying the fun of clapping together, giggling alongside Raghav.

grounding: Shows a toddler believing his clap made the timed lights come on, unable yet to separate his gesture from the physical world.

passage: On Sankranti morning in a village near Belgaum, Raghav sat on Devika didi's lap on the roof. Raghav puffed his cheeks and blew at the red kite. Just then the wind lifted it into the sky. "Raghav blow!" he gasped. He blew at the green kite. Nothing. He blew again, red in the face. Devika didi put his hand on the string. "Feel the wind, Raghav." He blew once more, just in case.

qa.q: Where did Raghav sit on Sankranti morning?
qa.a: On Devika didi's lap on the roof.

qa.q: Why did Raghav blow so hard at the green kite?
qa.a: He felt excited and sure his blowing had made the red kite fly, so he expected it to work again.

qa.q: What did Devika didi do that helps a toddler learn?
qa.a: She put his hand on the string so he could feel the wind pulling, a simple, gentle way to show what really lifts the kite.

qa.q: How might Devika didi feel watching Raghav blow at the kite?
qa.a: She seems amused and tender, enjoying his belief while starting to show him the wind.

grounding: Shows a toddler during Sankranti believing his breath makes a kite fly, not yet separating his action from the wind.

passage:
First snow had fallen on Sapporo. Nour, two, stood at the window with his mother Yuki.

A toy car sat on the floor. Nour waved his hand at it. "Go!"

The car didn't move.

He waved harder. "Go, go!"

Yuki gave the car a gentle push with her foot. It rolled across the floor.

Nour squealed and waved again, sure his hand had done it.

Yuki laughed and pushed it once more.

qa.q: What did Nour wave his hand at?
qa.a: A toy car.

qa.q: Why did Nour squeal and wave again?
qa.a: He felt delighted and sure that his wave had made the car move.

qa.q: What did Yuki do that kept the game joyful?
qa.a: She played along by gently pushing the car, letting Nour enjoy the moment.

qa.q: How might Yuki feel watching Nour wave at the car?
qa.a: Yuki probably feels amused and fond, enjoying his belief in his own magic.

grounding: A toddler believes his wave makes a toy car move, not yet separating thought from the physical world.

passage:
Monday, during Diwali week. Kamal, two, pointed at the lamp. "Off!" His aunt Nikita switched it off at the wall. Kamal gasped.

Wednesday. He pointed at the ceiling fan. "Stop!" It kept spinning. He frowned and pointed harder.

Friday. He pointed at the diyas on the balcony. "On!" Nikita lit them. Kamal clapped, sure he'd made the lights appear.

qa.q: What did Kamal point at on Wednesday?
qa.a: The ceiling fan.

qa.q: Why did Kamal frown and point harder at the fan?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and a bit cross, because he believed his pointing should make it stop.

qa.q: How could Nikita gently help Kamal over time?
qa.a: She could show him the switch and say "I press it" while he watches, so he slowly learns what really makes things work.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when Kamal claps at the diyas?
qa.a: Nikita probably feels amused and warm, seeing how sure he is of his magic.

grounding: A toddler believes his pointing and words make lights and fans obey, not yet separating thought from the physical world.

passage:
Monsoon rain was pouring on their Pune flat. Vijay, two, sat on the floor while his grandfather Kishore read the newspaper.

Vijay closed his eyes tight. "Rain, stop!"

Outside, the rain kept pouring.

He opened his eyes, frowned, and closed them again. "Stop!"

A minute later, the rain slowed to a drizzle.

Vijay jumped up. "I did it!"

Kishore smiled and lifted him to the window. "Look, the clouds are moving."

qa.q: What did Vijay shout with his eyes closed?
qa.a: "Rain, stop!"

qa.q: Why did Vijay jump up and shout "I did it!"?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, believing his wish had made the rain stop.

qa.q: What did Kishore do that was gentle and truthful?
qa.a: He smiled and showed Vijay the moving clouds, giving a simple real reason without mocking him.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel watching Vijay try to stop the rain?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels amused and tender toward his grandson.

grounding: A toddler believes his wish stopped the rain, not yet separating thought from the physical world.

passage:
"Pranav, look, Diwali lights!"
Pranav waved both hands at the dark balcony. Click. The lights blinked on.
"I did it!" He waved again, harder.
Harsha bhaiya laughed. "No, the timer did it."
Pranav shook his head. "Me! Bye-bye, lights!" He waved. The lights stayed on.
"Again!" He waved and waved.
Amma crouched beside him. "The switch box turns them on, see? Shall we press it together?"
Pranav pressed. Dark. Pressed again. Bright!
"Me!" he shouted.

qa.q: What turned the lights on, according to Harsha bhaiya?
qa.a: The timer.

qa.q: Why does Pranav shout "I did it!"?
qa.a: He is delighted and believes his wave made the lights come on; at his age a wish or gesture feels like it can make things happen.

qa.q: How does Amma help Pranav?
qa.a: She shows him the switch box and lets him press it, giving a simple true cause he can feel, without mocking him.

qa.q: How might Harsha bhaiya feel about Pranav's claim?
qa.a: He finds it funny and wants to correct it, and may be amused that Pranav keeps waving.

grounding: A toddler believes his wave turned on the Diwali lights.

passage: Daycare note. At snack time, Sahil stared hard at the toy car on the shelf and said, "Come, car!" Just then his cousin Noor bumped the shelf, and the car rolled off. Sahil gasped and clapped: "I did!" He tried again with the ball. Nothing. Noor giggled. "I pushed it, silly." Sahil frowned. I rolled the car to him and said, "Hands make cars move. Let's push." He pushed and cheered. At pickup I told his mother about his "magic"; she laughed.

qa.q: What did Sahil say to the toy car?
qa.a: "Come, car!"

qa.q: Why did Sahil clap and say "I did!"?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, believing his stare and words made the car move, since he can't yet separate thoughts from what happens.

qa.q: How did the caregiver respond helpfully?
qa.a: By rolling the car to him and saying "hands make cars move", then letting him push it: a simple true cause, with no scolding.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor when Sahil claims the credit?
qa.a: Noor finds it funny and tells him she pushed it, perhaps enjoying knowing the real reason.

grounding: A toddler believes his wish made a toy car roll, when his cousin had bumped the shelf.

passage: On the village verandah, rain drummed on the tin roof. Little Pranav pointed at the sky and shouted, "Stop!" A minute later, the rain slowed and stopped. Pranav's eyes went round. "I stopped it!" His big sister Minakshi, folding clothes, burst out laughing. "You're not the rain king!" Pranav's lip trembled. Aaji pulled him onto her lap. "The clouds went away by themselves. But you said it very loudly." Pranav pointed again. "Sun, come!"

qa.q: What did Pranav shout at the sky?
qa.a: "Stop!"

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the rain stopped?
qa.a: He felt amazed and powerful, his eyes round, believing his shout had stopped the rain.

qa.q: How did Aaji respond?
qa.a: She pulled him onto her lap and gently said the clouds went away by themselves, while praising his loud voice instead of mocking him.

qa.q: What would change if Aaji had laughed too?
qa.a: Pranav might feel ashamed and hurt, since his lip was already trembling, instead of comforted.

grounding: A toddler believes his shout stopped the rain.

passage:
At the supermarket entrance in Nairobi, little Bilal stood in front of the glass doors and waved both hands. Whoosh, the doors slid open.
He gasped and looked up at Mama. He stepped back and waved again. Whoosh.
"I did it!" he shouted, flapping his arms.
His big cousin Wanjiru giggled. "It's the door's eye up there, Bilal, not your hands."
Bilal didn't listen. He waved at the trolley, then at a balloon, waiting for them to move too.

qa.q: What happened when Bilal waved at the glass doors?
qa.a: The doors slid open.

qa.q: What did Bilal feel when the doors opened a second time?
qa.a: He felt amazed and proud, sure that his waving had made the doors move.

qa.q: How could Mama gently help Bilal with the door?
qa.a: She could let him enjoy it, then show him that the doors open when anyone walks near, even with hands kept still.

qa.q: How does Wanjiru see Bilal's waving?
qa.a: Wanjiru finds it funny and knows the door's eye opens it, not Bilal's hands.

grounding: Shows a toddler believing his wave makes doors and toys move.
